lines: Mirehaven. Four thousand of us, and not one square foot of ground under any of it.
Everything you can stand on here, somebody paid for and somebody maintains.
Walk where the lamps are and do not lean on anything you did not test first.
Three hundred and eleven lamps between the Landing and the third row.
I light them, my mother lit them, and her mother put half of them up.
You can see the town from four miles out on a clear night. There are no clear nights.
You can walk to the East Stage. It takes forty minutes and it is a beautiful walk.
Or I can put you across in ninety seconds for nothing, because I am going anyway.
Most people walk. I have never understood most people.
There was a Mirehaven before this one, and it was on the ground, and the ground went.
My grandmother's grandmother watched the water come up over her doorstep and stay.
So we built up. That is the whole history of this town in one sentence.
You are looking at the Rock. Everybody looks at the Rock.
It was here before us and it was cut before us, and we built out from it because it is dry.
Whatever made that cut did not use tools. Do not ask me what I think about that.
They went down four days ago with lamps and cases and a paper from somewhere.
I am the warden of this rock and I could not tell them no. That is a new feeling.
If you go down after them, go down with somebody. I mean that kindly.
The Sanctum is shut, and it has been shut since before anybody in this town was born.
There is no lock on it. There is no door on it. It is simply shut.
Something in there decides, and it has been deciding no for three thousand years.
The Foundation is conducting a hydrological survey of the wetland. It is quite routine.
Sanctum access is restricted for the safety of the public. That is also quite routine.
You have questions. I have a form. Neither of us is going to enjoy this.
Flat bottom, square ends, pitch inside and out, and you pole it, you do not row it.
Four hundred of them in this town and I have built or mended near half.
A punt is a house that goes places. Treat it like a house and it lasts thirty years.
Nets rot out here in a season. Everything rots out here in a season.
Pitch, tar, oil, salt. Half of what this town spends is spent on staying put.
The stage is where the reed dries. Two months in the wind and it goes on a roof.
Every roof you can see came out of the beds you walked through to get here.
You want to know what Mirehaven is made of? It is made of the road you came in on.
Everyone says do not go under the decks. I go under the decks.
There are stone bits down there. Square ones. With lines cut in them.
Grandad says they are old. Grandad says lots of things are old and this is different.
At night the water goes green. Not all of it. Just where the Kin are.
You can see them from up here, moving about under the boards, all lit up.
Mum says it is only Kin. I know it is only Kin. It is still the best thing here.
Every pile under this row I have been down to and put my hands on.
Three years ago we cut every one of them off level and built the deck a foot higher.
Cost us a fortune. Water has not come over since. Ask me if it was worth it.
The third row is the poor end, if you are wondering. It is also the quiet end.
Nobody walks down here on the way to anywhere, because it is not on the way to anywhere.
That suits us. It has suited us for a hundred and forty years.
Your friend came through. Loud one. Beat two of the Hall crew before lunch.
Then he went and sat on the Rock and looked at that cut in the stone for an hour.
Did not say a word to anybody. Then he went down to the causeway to wait, he said.
Four thousand people and everybody knows everybody, which is not always a virtue.
